items: Dependence on specific substrate architecture (pyridine-alkyne eneyne tethers and, for α-C–C cleavage, a cyclopropyl bridge) may limit generality.

Proposed 8π electrocyclization and “tricyclic metal-carbene” intermediacy, while plausible, lack direct experimental or computational corroboration (e.g., no carbene trapping, spectroscopy, or DFT analysis).
Reaction temperatures are relatively high and, for the α-C–C cleavage, require CHCl3 and a silver salt with a phase-transfer agent; sustainability and cost could be concerns.
The origin and control of diastereoselectivity/stereochemical outcomes are not deeply analyzed.
Functional group tolerance for strongly coordinating, protic, or redox-sensitive moieties (free amines, aldehydes, acids, nitro groups) is insufficiently explored or documented.
The α-C–C cleavage manifold is mostly limited to cyclopropanes; other strained motifs (cyclobutanes, vinylcyclopropanes, donor–acceptor cyclopropanes) are not examined.
Limited kinetics, mechanistic rate studies, or competition experiments; no KIE data for α-C–H cleavage; no Hammett analysis to probe electronic effects.
The role of water/protons in the two protonation events is inferred but not definitively established (e.g., water content control, molecular sieves, alternative proton sources).
Some nomenclature and abbreviations (e.g., CuTc vs CuTC, TEBA) could be standardized/defined on first use; a few grammatical and formatting inconsistencies remain.
The mechanistic figure would benefit from explicit metal oxidation states/ligands and clearer bookkeeping of charges and protonation steps.
Tables are referenced but not shown in the main text excerpt; clarity about yields, selectivity, and conditions should be consolidated.

While the paper cites foundational literature on enyne cycloisomerizations, carbenes, and 8π electrocyclizations, it could better contextualize against recent advances in: (i) gold/copper-catalyzed formation and reactivity of vinyl metal zwitterions in N-fused systems; (ii) medium-ring construction via electrocyclizations or sigmatropic rearrangements; (iii) ring-opening chemistry of cyclopropylcarbinyl cations under transition-metal catalysis.
Preliminary biological or physicochemical characterization (beyond synthetic access) of the new NCPC scaffold is not provided, which would strengthen the significance claims for medicinal chemistry.
Lack of quantitative electrochemical metrics (e.g., electrode potentials, faradaic efficiency, current–time/potential–time profiles) limits assessment of energy efficiency and scalability.
Undivided-cell operation in HF-rich media raises questions about cathodic processes, gas evolution, and potential competitive reactions that are not characterized.
The influence of mass transport and cell geometry on selectivity and rate is not discussed, though such factors can be decisive in anodic radical-cation chemistry.
No kinetic data, rate laws, or competition experiments to substantiate the claimed kinetic selectivity (MeOH vs Et3N·3HF) or the stepwise radical-to-carbocation sequence.
Limited stereochemical analysis for disubstituted/tri-substituted cyclopropanes; mechanistic stereochemical implications of three-electron SN2 opening are underexplored.
Oxyfluorination with ethers invokes oxonium intermediates; more direct evidence (e.g., 18O labeling, interception studies) would solidify this mechanistic branch.
Some yields are reported as GC/NMR without consistent isolated yields across the board, making cross-comparison harder.
Minor inconsistencies in reaction times and scales between entries and figures could be clarified to help reproducibility assessment.

A more explicit, side-by-side comparison with leading hypervalent iodine and photoredox methods for 1,3-difunctionalization (scope breadth, functional-group tolerance, scalability, cost, and safety) would better position the contribution.
Discussion of alternative mechanistic possibilities (e.g., direct fluorination pathways, chain processes) is relatively brief given the complexity of fluorination under electrochemical conditions.
Selectivity profiling is limited to two PLA2 comparators; broader off-target profiling (COX/LOX enzyme panels, kinases, receptors, transporters) is not reported.
The thiazolyl ketone warhead may present covalency/chemical reactivity concerns; glutathione adduction and thiol-reactivity data are lacking.
Plasma stability is reported, but solubility, permeability, metabolic stability (microsomes/S9), and CYP/hERG liabilities are not disclosed.

The mechanistic claim of PRC2-dependent transcriptional repression and ROS-mediated lethality is primarily correlative within the provided text; direct epigenetic and genetic validation is not shown here (e.g., H3K27me3 ChIP-seq, EZH2 dependency, PLA2G4A genetic perturbation).
Limited in vivo efficacy/PK-PD data: no leukemia models, tumor eicosanoid biomarker modulation, or tolerability data are provided.
Cell line screen size (n=66) is modest and may underpower genetic association analyses; multiple testing correction details and validation on independent cohorts are not fully described.
Table 1 “Human plasma stability” column uses unclear units/notations (e.g., “x”, “*”, “ND¤”) without in-text footnote definitions; timepoints differ (20–25 h) without rationale.
Diastereomeric/stereochemical issues for α-methyl analogs are not discussed; activity may be enantiomer-dependent.
The relation between XI(50) values and cellular IC50s needs clearer discussion of interfacial assay conditions and translation to cell systems.

Limited comparison with other recent small-molecule cPLA2α inhibitors beyond legacy references; benchmarking against state-of-the-art tool compounds across standardized biochemical and cellular assays would strengthen claims.
Prior reports linking PLA2G4A to epigenetic regulation or ROS homeostasis are not synthesized; the novelty claim would benefit from deeper contextualization and explicit contrasts.

Dependence on Assumption 0.2 (small noise-to-signal ratio) is strong for microbiome data where technical and sampling noise can be substantial; practical diagnostics or robustness analyses are not provided.

Handling of zeros conflates structural and sampling zeros—log-transformation is applied only when Mij=1, but in real data Mij is unknown; the resulting pairwise-complete approach may induce bias for rare taxa.

Distance correlation is unsigned; the recommendation to “borrow” the sign from linear correlation may be unstable in small n or weakly monotone nonlinear regimes; lack of a principled signed nonlinear dependence measure.
The cross-ecosystem “scale invariance” claim is asserted but not fully formalized; conditions for identifiability and comparability of Cj across ecosystems are not rigorously discussed.
Nonlinear baselines such as HSIC, MIC/MICe, or signed-kernel/energy-based measures are not included; this weakens claims of superiority for nonlinear detection.
P-value filtering is used without family-wise/FDR control; multiple-testing calibration is essential in network inference, especially with small n.
Simulation details on how differential sequencing efficiencies and sampling fractions are generated and estimated are deferred, limiting reproducibility of the bias-correction validation.
No sensitivity analyses for violations of assumptions (e.g., degree of noise, zero-inflation rates, co-occurrence prevalence thresholds, or misestimation of S and C).
Estimation of variances for the weighting scheme wj and practical computation in the presence of many zeros are not fully specified; guidance on robust estimation would help.
The computational complexity of distance correlation and strategies to scale to larger n (e.g., O(n log n) algorithms) are not discussed.
Closely related structural-zero covariance/precision estimation under pairwise-complete strategies (e.g., Kaul et al., 2016) is not cited, though the setup is similar.
Modern nonlinear dependence and energy/kernel-based methods (HSIC; fast unbiased dCor estimators) are not discussed; fast dCor computation (Huo & Székely, 2014) is relevant for scalability.

The model relies on simplified impedance elements (ideal capacitors) and neglects parasitic capacitances, Faradaic/leakage pathways, and diffusion-related Warburg/CPE behavior known to be relevant in physiological EIS.

The current-splitting factor f_OECT is treated as an empirical fit parameter, which weakens predictive power; its dependence on geometry and bias is acknowledged but not independently measured or modeled.
The electrolyte impedance Z_el is treated at a macroscopic level; potential frequency dispersion of the medium and non-ideal double layers are not explicitly included.
No quantitative noise spectra or SNR improvements are reported, despite the central motivation of gain for improving measurement fidelity.
Validation is limited to one cell line and a single electrolyte; broader exploration of media conductivity, ionic strength, or temperature dependence is absent.

The microparticle model captures geometric current constriction but omits membrane capacitance/seal resistance effects characteristic of cells; additional validation linking microparticle- and cell-induced impedance pathways would strengthen the analogy.
Limited statistics on device-to-device and cell-to-cell variability; the reported gain is compelling but its robustness across batches and conditions is not fully quantified.

Some symbols/assumptions (e.g., the exact derivation of VG* and its dependence on Z_el and Z_ch, and the mapping from microparticle distance to ΔZ_el via the proportionality p) could be detailed more thoroughly or supported by simulations.
The choice and extraction of Z_el from microelectrode fits is only briefly referenced; reporting the equivalent circuit used and fit quality would aid reproducibility.

The analysis would benefit from connecting to cell–substrate impedance models that explicitly treat finite/small electrodes relative to cell size (e.g., analytical treatments akin to Shiozawa & Uno, 2022), to position the microparticle model within single-cell EIS theory.

Diffusive/Warburg-like extracellular effects observed in biological media (e.g., non-ohmic frequency dependence) are not discussed; incorporating or bounding such effects would clarify applicability across preparations.
The results could be contextualized with recent high-gm electrolyte-gated transistor architectures (e.g., vertical nanogap EGTs) that may further increase gain within the same framework.
